README.md:526:### Checkpoint Remote
README.md:528:By default, checkpoint data rides along with your own pushes — but only to **one** remote, the elected checkpoint sync remote. Entire picks it in this order:
README.md:530:1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`, if set. This is fail-closed: if it names a remote that isn't configured, checkpoints don't sync.
README.md:531:2. A remote captured from your own habits: the first push whose target matches the branch's declared push destination elects that remote, announces it on stderr, and carries the checkpoints. The first capture sticks.
README.md:536:A push to any *other* remote carries no checkpoint data. `entire status` shows the current destination, where it came from, and how many checkpoints are unpushed. This matters if you push code to several remotes: checkpoints go to exactly one of them.
README.md:538:If instead you want checkpoint data in a separate repo (e.g., a private repo for a public project), configure `checkpoint_remote` with a structured provider and repo. A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` is addressed directly and is exempt from the single-remote election above:
README.md:543:    "checkpoint_remote": {
README.md:545:      "repo": "myorg/checkpoints-private"
README.md:554:entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private
README.md:557:Entire derives the git URL automatically using the same protocol (SSH or HTTPS) as your push remote. It will:
README.md:559:- Fetch existing checkpoint data locally if the remote has it and you don't (one-time)
README.md:560:- Push checkpoint data to the checkpoint repo instead of your default push remote
README.md:561:- Ignore the setting if it looks inherited rather than yours, and fall back to `origin` (or, failing that, the remote you are pushing to). `checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so cloning or forking a project inherits it — without this, a contributor's session data would be pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo. A setting is treated as yours when it lives in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`, or when your `origin` **and every push URL** of the remote you are pushing to are owned by the same account or org as the checkpoint repo. Requiring the push destination too covers contributors who cloned the upstream repo and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project rather than to them; requiring every push URL covers mirror-style remotes that fan out to several repositories
README.md:562:- If your checkpoint repo is owned by a different account or org than `origin`, configure it in `.entire/settings.local.json` so it is always honored
README.md:567:`ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` allows you to provide a dedicated token for checkpoint repository operations, without modifying the credentials used for your primary repository.
README.md:569:When this environment variable is set, Entire behaves as follows:
README.md:571:- Injects the token into HTTPS Git operations used for checkpoint fetch and push
README.md:572:- If `checkpoint_remote` is configured:
README.md:573:  - Prefers an HTTPS URL for the checkpoint remote when a token is present, even if the repository’s `origin` uses SSH
README.md:574:- If `checkpoint_remote` is not configured:
README.md:576:- If `checkpoint_remote` configuration cannot be loaded:
README.md:578:  - If `origin` is a valid SSH or HTTPS Git remote, Entire converts it to an HTTPS URL to enable token-based authentication
README.md:582:When enabled, Entire automatically generates AI summaries for checkpoints at commit time. Summaries capture intent, outcome, learnings, friction points, and open items from the session.
README.md:594:Summaries are also generated on demand, with or without this setting, by `entire checkpoint explain --generate`.
README.md:596:**Which agent writes them.** By default Claude Code (`claude` on your `PATH`, model `sonnet`). Set a different one with `summary_generation.provider` — `claude-code`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `cursor`, `gemini`, or `pi`, plus an optional `summary_generation.model` hint:
README.md:599:entire configure --summarize-provider codex
README.md:611:Local settings override project settings field-by-field. `entire status --detailed` shows the state of each settings file.
README.md:615:- The `checkpoints` block is **replaced wholesale** by the local one, not deep-merged — it selects a backend, so a half-merged block would be meaningless.
README.md:616:- A `settings.local.json` that is **tracked in git** is ignored entirely, and Entire tells you to `git rm --cached` it. `.gitignore` doesn't apply to an already-tracked path, so a committed local file would otherwise override project settings for everyone who clones.
README.md:620:- Codex hooks are enabled by default (codex-cli 0.124.0+), so enabling Entire for Codex only installs `.codex/hooks.json` — no `config.toml` is needed and Entire never creates one. If an older Entire version left a `.codex/config.toml` behind and your repo lives inside `~/.codex/agents`, delete that file to stop Codex's "malformed agent role definition" startup warning.
README.md:621:- Entire supports Cursor IDE and Cursor Agent CLI tool. Commands (`doctor`, `status` etc.) work the same as all other agents.
README.md:622:- Entire supports Copilot CLI, but not Copilot in VS Code, in other IDEs, or on github.com.
README.md:623:- Entire supports Pi coding agent (Preview). Pi uses a TypeScript extension instead of a JSON hook config. Subagent capture is not currently available.
README.md:627:**Your session transcripts are stored in your git repository**, in the [per-checkpoint refs](#checkpoint-storage) described above. If your repository is public, this data is visible to anyone.
README.md:629:Entire automatically redacts detected secrets (API keys, tokens, credentials) from transcripts and metadata before writing a checkpoint, but redaction is best-effort.
README.md:631:The temporary shadow branches used during a session get the same redaction for transcripts and metadata, but their **code-file snapshots are raw blobs of your working tree**, so a secret hardcoded in your source appears unredacted there. Entire never pushes shadow branches — don't push them manually. See [docs/security-and-privacy.md](docs/security-and-privacy.md) for the full picture, including the configurable scanner layers, opt-in PII redaction, and the OpenAI Privacy Filter pass.

agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:5:Kilo Code is a fork of OpenCode with a `@kilocode/plugin` API that exposes session lifecycle events on its internal event bus. Plugins are TypeScript/JavaScript modules loaded at startup from `.kilo/plugins/` and run on Bun. The integration installs a project plugin that subscribes to the bus and forwards five lifecycle hooks (`session-start`, `turn-start`, `turn-end`, `compaction`, `session-end`) to the Entire CLI. The plugin uses Kilo's native event bus directly — `session.idle` is deprecated upstream and `session.status` with `status.type === "idle"` is the reliable turn-end signal in both interactive and `kilo run` modes.

agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:104:- **Resume restore is EXPERIMENTAL / incomplete.** Kilo keeps sessions in a global store (`~/.local/share/kilo/kilo.db`) keyed by session id, not in `.entire/`. `entire resume` restores the transcript to `.entire/tmp/kilo/<id>.json` and prints `kilo run --session <id>`, but Kilo only reads its own store — so resume works **only while Kilo still has the session locally**. Restoring a session Entire has but Kilo does not (after `kilo session delete`, a fresh clone, or another machine) is **not yet supported**: it would require importing the session back into Kilo via `kilo import <file>` (Kilo exposes `kilo export [id]` / `kilo import <file>` for this). That needs the durable artifact to be Kilo's native export blob rather than the analysis-oriented JSONL stored today, and is tracked as future work. Everything else (checkpointing, attribution, summaries, transcript analysis) is unaffected. The agent is `is_preview: true` accordingly.
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:105:- Kilo plugins do not load when `KILO_PURE=1` is set. The plugin must not assume that env is unset; if it is set, hooks never fire and `are-hooks-installed` still returns true (file exists).
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:106:- The transcript is materialized by `prepare-transcript` (Go side, via `kilo session show --format json` — see `command_runner.go`), which Entire calls before reading, mirroring the OpenCode parent. The plugin's `turn-end` fires **synchronously** and carries only `session_id` + `model`: `kilo run` exits on the same idle event, so an awaited in-plugin fetch could be cancelled before the hook runs. Turn-end payloads that do carry messages are still honored, but an empty message set never overwrites an existing transcript.
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:107:- `session.idle` is deprecated upstream and not reliably emitted in `kilo run` mode. The plugin subscribes to `session.status` and filters on `status.type === "idle"` for turn-end.
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:108:- Sub-sessions (Kilo subagent threads) are filtered out at `session.created` time by checking `info.parentID`. Subagent activity inside the parent session is still captured because the parent session JSON includes all parts.

build/README.md:1:# External Agents for Entire CLI
build/README.md:3:This repository contains standalone external agent binaries that extend the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli) with support for additional AI coding agents.
build/README.md:7:External agents are standalone binaries (named `entire-agent-<name>`) that teach Entire CLI how to work with AI coding agents it doesn't natively support. When an external agent is installed on your `PATH`, Entire discovers it automatically and gains the ability to:
build/README.md:9:- **Create checkpoints** during AI coding sessions so you can rewind mistakes
build/README.md:10:- **Capture transcripts** of what the AI agent did and why
build/README.md:11:- **Install hooks** so the AI agent's lifecycle events (start, stop, commit) flow through Entire
build/README.md:13:External agents communicate with Entire CLI via subcommands that accept and return JSON over stdin/stdout. See the [external agent protocol spec](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md) for the full interface.

Project hooks require folder trust (`/hooks-trust` or `--trust`) before they execute, and until the folder is trusted Grok skips them silently, so nothing is captured.

agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:39:- IDE hook command form: macOS/Linux use `sh -c '<command> </dev/null'`; Windows uses `cmd /c "<command> <NUL"` so the parent `entire` CLI process inherits a closed stdin (Kiro IDE on Windows leaves stdin open, and the adapter's 100ms stdin timeout only covers the agent binary, not the CLI parent)
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:42:- Session ID source: `parse-hook` resolves identity in this order: (1) explicit IDE session ID (`session_id` / `sessionId` / `chatSessionId`) in the hook payload — populates both `entire_session_id` and `ide_session_id`; (2) explicit CLI `conversation_id` in the payload — populates `entire_session_id` and `conversation_id` only, leaving `ide_session_id` empty so transcript capture skips the IDE path (otherwise a repo with leftover IDE workspace data would silently checkpoint an unrelated IDE chat for what is actually a CLI turn); (3) the most-recently-modified `<sessionId>.json` file in the IDE workspace-sessions directory — Kiro writes the user's prompt or assistant's response to the active chat's transcript file before invoking the hook, so file mtime is the closest signal to "which chat tab fired"; the IDE session UUID is used as both `ide_session_id` and `entire_session_id`; (4) repo-global `kiro-active-session` cache (Kiro CLI / non-IDE flow); (5) CLI `conversation_id` queried from the SQLite DB; (6) a generated Entire ID
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:43:- Session cache: `.entire/tmp/kiro-active-session` is used exclusively for the Kiro-CLI (non-IDE) flow. IDE chats aren't cached as a "current session" because re-deriving from `<sessionId>.json` mtime each turn is what lets tab-switching scenarios resolve correctly
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:44:- Active turn cache: `.entire/tmp/kiro-active-turn` holds the IDE session ID for the in-flight turn — written at `user-prompt-submit`, read by `post-tool-use` and `stop`, cleared at end of `stop`. README.md:181:A **session** represents a complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps.
README.md:183:The session ID is the unique identifier the agent itself provides — Entire never mints its own — so an ID you see in `entire session list` is the same one the agent uses. README.md:185:Sessions are stored separately from your code commits, in the repo's checkpoint storage.
README.md:187:### Checkpoints
README.md:189:A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.
README.md:191:Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.
README.md:193:**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.
README.md:195:### Checkpoint Storage
README.md:197:Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:
README.md:200:refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>
README.md:203:The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.
README.md:205:Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.
README.md:207:`entire enable` sets this up; there is nothing to configure. It is recorded in `.entire/settings.json` as:

README.md:250:Entire uses a manual-commit strategy that keeps your git history clean:

README.md:258:Entire works seamlessly with [git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree). Each worktree has independent session tracking, so you can run multiple AI sessions in different worktrees without conflicts.

README.md:526:### Checkpoint Remote
README.md:528:By default, checkpoint data rides along with your own pushes — but only to **one** remote, the elected checkpoint sync remote. Entire picks it in this order:
README.md:530:1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`, if set. This is fail-closed: if it names a remote that isn't configured, checkpoints don't sync.
README.md:531:2. A remote captured from your own habits: the first push whose target matches the branch's declared push destination elects that remote, announces it on stderr, and carries the checkpoints. The first capture sticks.
README.md:536:A push to any *other* remote carries no checkpoint data. `entire status` shows the current destination, where it came from, and how many checkpoints are unpushed. This matters if you push code to several remotes: checkpoints go to exactly one of them.
README.md:538:If instead you want checkpoint data in a separate repo (e.g., a private repo for a public project), configure `checkpoint_remote` with a structured provider and repo. A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` is addressed directly and is exempt from the single-remote election above:
README.md:543:    "checkpoint_remote": {
README.md:545:      "repo": "myorg/checkpoints-private"
README.md:554:entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private
README.md:557:Entire derives the git URL automatically using the same protocol (SSH or HTTPS) as your push remote. It will:
README.md:559:- Fetch existing checkpoint data locally if the remote has it and you don't (one-time)
README.md:560:- Push checkpoint data to the checkpoint repo instead of your default push remote
README.md:561:- Ignore the setting if it looks inherited rather than yours, and fall back to `origin` (or, failing that, the remote you are pushing to). `checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so cloning or forking a project inherits it — without this, a contributor's session data would be pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo. A setting is treated as yours when it lives in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`, or when your `origin` **and every push URL** of the remote you are pushing to are owned by the same account or org as the checkpoint repo. Requiring the push destination too covers contributors who cloned the upstream repo and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project rather than to them; requiring every push URL covers mirror-style remotes that fan out to several repositories
README.md:562:- If your checkpoint repo is owned by a different account or org than `origin`, configure it in `.entire/settings.local.json` so it is always honored
README.md:567:`ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` allows you to provide a dedicated token for checkpoint repository operations, without modifying the credentials used for your primary repository.
README.md:569:When this environment variable is set, Entire behaves as follows:
README.md:571:- Injects the token into HTTPS Git operations used for checkpoint fetch and push
README.md:572:- If `checkpoint_remote` is configured:
README.md:573:  - Prefers an HTTPS URL for the checkpoint remote when a token is present, even if the repository’s `origin` uses SSH
README.md:574:- If `checkpoint_remote` is not configured:
README.md:576:- If `checkpoint_remote` configuration cannot be loaded:
README.md:578:  - If `origin` is a valid SSH or HTTPS Git remote, Entire converts it to an HTTPS URL to enable token-based authentication

agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:5:Kilo Code is a fork of OpenCode with a `@kilocode/plugin` API that exposes session lifecycle events on its internal event bus. Plugins are TypeScript/JavaScript modules loaded at startup from `.kilo/plugins/` and run on Bun. The integration installs a project plugin that subscribes to the bus and forwards five lifecycle hooks (`session-start`, `turn-start`, `turn-end`, `compaction`, `session-end`) to the Entire CLI. The plugin uses Kilo's native event bus directly — `session.idle` is deprecated upstream and `session.status` with `status.type === "idle"` is the reliable turn-end signal in both interactive and `kilo run` modes.

agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:104:- **Resume restore is EXPERIMENTAL / incomplete.** Kilo keeps sessions in a global store (`~/.local/share/kilo/kilo.db`) keyed by session id, not in `.entire/`. `entire resume` restores the transcript to `.entire/tmp/kilo/<id>.json` and prints `kilo run --session <id>`, but Kilo only reads its own store — so resume works **only while Kilo still has the session locally**. Restoring a session Entire has but Kilo does not (after `kilo session delete`, a fresh clone, or another machine) is **not yet supported**: it would require importing the session back into Kilo via `kilo import <file>` (Kilo exposes `kilo export [id]` / `kilo import <file>` for this). That needs the durable artifact to be Kilo's native export blob rather than the analysis-oriented JSONL stored today, and is tracked as future work. Everything else (checkpointing, attribution, summaries, transcript analysis) is unaffected. The agent is `is_preview: true` accordingly.
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:105:- Kilo plugins do not load when `KILO_PURE=1` is set. The plugin must not assume that env is unset; if it is set, hooks never fire and `are-hooks-installed` still returns true (file exists).
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:106:- The transcript is materialized by `prepare-transcript` (Go side, via `kilo session show --format json` — see `command_runner.go`), which Entire calls before reading, mirroring the OpenCode parent. The plugin's `turn-end` fires **synchronously** and carries only `session_id` + `model`: `kilo run` exits on the same idle event, so an awaited in-plugin fetch could be cancelled before the hook runs. Turn-end payloads that do carry messages are still honored, but an empty message set never overwrites an existing transcript.
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:107:- `session.idle` is deprecated upstream and not reliably emitted in `kilo run` mode. The plugin subscribes to `session.status` and filters on `status.type === "idle"` for turn-end.
agents/entire-agent-kilo/AGENT.md:108:- Sub-sessions (Kilo subagent threads) are filtered out at `session.created` time by checking `info.parentID`. Subagent activity inside the parent session is still captured because the parent session JSON includes all parts.

build/README.md:1:# External Agents for Entire CLI
build/README.md:3:This repository contains standalone external agent binaries that extend the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli) with support for additional AI coding agents.
build/README.md:7:External agents are standalone binaries (named `entire-agent-<name>`) that teach Entire CLI how to work with AI coding agents it doesn't natively support. When an external agent is installed on your `PATH`, Entire discovers it automatically and gains the ability to:
build/README.md:9:- **Create checkpoints** during AI coding sessions so you can rewind mistakes
build/README.md:10:- **Capture transcripts** of what the AI agent did and why
build/README.md:11:- **Install hooks** so the AI agent's lifecycle events (start, stop, commit) flow through Entire
build/README.md:13:External agents communicate with Entire CLI via subcommands that accept and return JSON over stdin/stdout. See the [external agent protocol spec](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md) for the full interface.
build/README.md:19:| [Kiro](agents/entire-agent-kiro/) | `agents/entire-agent-kiro/` | Implemented — hooks + transcript analysis |
build/README.md:20:| [Amp](agents/entire-agent-amp/) | `agents/entire-agent-amp/` | Implemented — hooks + transcript analysis + token calculation + compact transcripts |
build/README.md:21:| [Qwen Code](agents/entire-agent-qwen/) | `agents/entire-agent-qwen/` | Implemented — hooks + transcript analysis + compact transcripts |
build/README.md:22:| [Grok Build](agents/entire-agent-grok/) | `agents/entire-agent-grok/` | Implemented — hooks + transcript analysis + compact transcripts |
build/README.md:23:| [Oh My Pi](agents/entire-agent-omp/) | `agents/entire-agent-omp/` | Implemented — hooks + transcript analysis + compact transcripts |
build/README.md:24:| [Kilo](agents/entire-agent-kilo/) | `agents/entire-agent-kilo/` | Implemented (preview) — hooks + transcript analysis + token calculation + compact transcripts |
build/README.md:30:External agent discovery is opt-in. Once an `entire-agent-<name>` binary is on your `PATH`, set `external_agents: true` in the repo's `.entire/settings.json` so Entire scans for it:
build/README.md:38:Without this flag, Entire ignores external agent binaries even when they're installed.

build/README.md:70:The adapter installs Grok command hooks in `.grok/hooks/entire.json` and reads native transcripts from `~/.grok/sessions/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>/chat_history.jsonl`. Project hooks require folder trust (`/hooks-trust` or `--trust`) before they execute, and until the folder is trusted Grok skips them silently, so nothing is captured.
build/README.md:72:Restored sessions can be resumed with `grok --resume <session-id>`, but not at full fidelity: Grok's `encrypted_content` reasoning state is stripped before storage, so a resumed session replays the conversation without its prior reasoning context. Sessions captured before this behaviour shipped cannot be resumed at all. See the [agent README](agents/entire-agent-grok/README.md#session-restore-and-resume).

agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:42:- Session ID source: `parse-hook` resolves identity in this order: (1) explicit IDE session ID (`session_id` / `sessionId` / `chatSessionId`) in the hook payload — populates both `entire_session_id` and `ide_session_id`; (2) explicit CLI `conversation_id` in the payload — populates `entire_session_id` and `conversation_id` only, leaving `ide_session_id` empty so transcript capture skips the IDE path (otherwise a repo with leftover IDE workspace data would silently checkpoint an unrelated IDE chat for what is actually a CLI turn); (3) the most-recently-modified `<sessionId>.json` file in the IDE workspace-sessions directory — Kiro writes the user's prompt or assistant's response to the active chat's transcript file before invoking the hook, so file mtime is the closest signal to "which chat tab fired"; the IDE session UUID is used as both `ide_session_id` and `entire_session_id`; (4) repo-global `kiro-active-session` cache (Kiro CLI / non-IDE flow); (5) CLI `conversation_id` queried from the SQLite DB; (6) a generated Entire ID
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:43:- Session cache: `.entire/tmp/kiro-active-session` is used exclusively for the Kiro-CLI (non-IDE) flow. IDE chats aren't cached as a "current session" because re-deriving from `<sessionId>.json` mtime each turn is what lets tab-switching scenarios resolve correctly
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:44:- Active turn cache: `.entire/tmp/kiro-active-turn` holds the IDE session ID for the in-flight turn — written at `user-prompt-submit`, read by `post-tool-use` and `stop`, cleared at end of `stop`. This binds an entire turn (prompt → tool uses → stop) to the chat that fired prompt-submit, so a tab switch mid-turn cannot cause stop to finalize against a different chat
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:45:- Per-chat trim offset: every IDE chat and every CLI `conversation_id` gets its own offset file (`.entire/tmp/kiro-transcript-offset-<key>.json`) so capturing one chat never trims another chat's history
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:46:- Per-chat tool-call capture: `post-tool-use` appends to a per-chat file (`.entire/tmp/kiro-tool-calls-<sanitized-id>.jsonl`) keyed by the active-turn cache; transcript capture reads only the current chat's file. The legacy global file is reserved for CLI-only flows where there is no IDE chat ID
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:49:- `kiro-active-turn` is a single repo-global file. Each prompt-submit overwrites it; each stop owner-checks before clearing. This is correct for the common cases — single chat, tab-switch mid-turn, sequential turns across tabs, and concurrent CLI+IDE activity (each side's payload lets the other flow stay isolated). It is best-effort under truly overlapping IDE turns (`A prompt → B prompt → A stop`): A's stop has no payload signal that distinguishes it from B's, so the resolver returns whichever IDE chat is currently in cache. The owner-check at clear time prevents A's stop from deleting B's binding, but A's session_id will still resolve to whatever the cache currently holds. Fixing this fully requires a per-turn signal in the hook payload from Kiro, which it does not provide today
agents/entire-agent-kiro/AGENT.md:50:- For the same reason, post-tool-use hooks during a truly overlapping IDE turn fall back to mtime-based active-chat detection when the cache holds the wrong chat. CLI flows are unaffected because they short-circuit on payload `conversation_id`

build/agents/entire-agent-omp/AGENT.md:35:`omp` 17.1.1 can supersede a `before_agent_start` notification before the agent loop begins, so the adapter waits for `agent_start` before opening the Entire turn.     64	// scanChatHistory parses a chat_history.jsonl stream leniently.
    65	//
    66	// Entire scopes a checkpoint by slicing the transcript from a mid-session
    67	// offset, which can cut the first line in half, and it reads the file while
    68	// Grok is still appending to it, which can leave a half-flushed final line.
    69	// Neither case is corruption, so an unparseable line is skipped rather than
    70	// failing the whole parse. Erroring here surfaces to the user as the summary
    71	// falling back to raw bytes and reporting "no content to summarize".
    72	func scanChatHistory(r io.Reader) ([]chatHistoryMessage, error) {
    73		var messages []chatHistoryMessage
    74		scanner := bufio.NewScanner(r)
    75		scanner.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 10*1024*1024)
    76		for scanner.Scan() {
    77			line := strings.TrimSpace(scanner.Text())
    78			if line == "" {
    79				continue
    80			}
    81			var message chatHistoryMessage
    82			if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(line), &message); err != nil {
    83				continue
    84			}
    85			messages = append(messages, message)
    86		}
    87		return messages, scanner.Err()

This repository includes a skill that guides you through building standalone external agent binaries for the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli). The current testing split is:

- Protocol compliance in `external-agents-tests`
- Lifecycle integration in this repo's `e2e/` harness
- Agent-specific unit tests in each `agents/entire-agent-*` module

# External Agent Builder

This repository includes a skill that guides you through building standalone external agent binaries for the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli). The current testing split is:

- Protocol compliance in `external-agents-tests`
- Lifecycle integration in this repo's `e2e/` harness
- Agent-specific unit tests in each `agents/entire-agent-*` module

## Available Commands

| Command | Skill file | Description |
|---------|-----------|-------------|
| Full pipeline | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` | Run all three phases sequentially |
| Research | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md` | Analyze the target agent's capabilities and map to the protocol |
| Write tests | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md` | Scaffold the binary and wire protocol compliance plus lifecycle coverage |
| Implement | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md` | Build the binary using protocol compliance first, lifecycle second, unit tests last |

## How to Use

When the user asks to "build an external agent", "create an agent binary", or "external agent plugin":

1. Read `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` for the full pipeline overview
2. Follow the three phases in order: research, write-tests, implement
3. Each phase has a dedicated skill file with detailed instructions
4. Keep reusable protocol checks out of this repo's `e2e/` directory. Add them to `external-agents-tests` instead.

The skill files reference Claude Code tool names. Map them to Codex equivalents:

| Skill references | Codex equivalent |

| `Skill` tool | Read the skill file directly |
| `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Bash` | Native Codex tools |

## Protocol Spec

The external agent protocol is defined at:
`https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md`

The command-line interface for Entire

Getting Started:
  To get started with Entire CLI, run 'entire enable' to enable
  session tracking in your repository, then 'entire agent add <name>'
  to install hooks for a specific agent. For more information, visit:
  https://docs.entire.io/overview


Environment Variables:
  ACCESSIBLE    Set to any value (e.g., ACCESSIBLE=1) to enable accessibility
                mode. This uses simpler text prompts instead of interactive
                TUI elements, which works better with screen readers.

Usage:
  entire [flags]
  entire [command]

Entire Setup:
  agent                      Manage agent integrations (add, remove, list)
  clean                      Clean up Entire session data
  configure                  Update Entire settings in the current repository
  disable                    Disable Entire in current repository
  doctor                     Diagnose and fix session issues
  enable                     Enable Entire in current repository
  plugin                     Manage Entire plugins (install, list, upgrade, search, remove)
  status                     Show Entire status

Sessions & Checkpoints:
  activity                   Show your activity overview
  checkpoint                 Inspect and search checkpoints
  dispatch                   Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work
  recap                      Summarize recent checkpoint activity
  search                     Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
  session                    Manage agent sessions tracked by Entire

Account:
  auth                       Manage authentication
  login                      Log in to Entire
  logout                     Log out of Entire

Control Plane:
  api                        Make an authenticated request to an Entire API and print the response
  grant                      Manage Entire access grants and org membership
  org                        Manage Entire organizations
  project                    Manage Entire projects
  repo                       Manage Entire repositories

Additional Commands:
  agent-help                 Machine-readable usage for coding agents (always matches the installed CLI)
  help                       Help about any command
  labs                       Explore experimental Entire workflows
  version                    Show build information

Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)
  -h, --help           help for entire
  -v, --version        version for entire

Use "entire [command] --help" for more information about a command.

item.stdout:
Rank which agents, skills, and tools have provenance over a code scope — who
and what has touched the given code.

The argument is either a single scope (a file or directory path) or a
natural-language query. A scope or query is required unless --staged is set,
which uses the staged file paths as scopes instead. Results come from the
entire-api cell keyed on the repo, so the repo must be mirrored.

Usage:
  entire experts [scope-or-query] [flags]

Examples:
  entire experts src/payments --json
  entire experts "who owns token refresh" --json
  entire experts --staged

Flags:
      --branch string   Branch to inspect
  -h, --help            help for experts
      --json            Print JSON
      --limit int       Maximum profiles to return (1–20; values above 20 are clamped) (default 8)
      --repo string     Repository as owner/repo
      --staged          Use staged file paths as scopes
      --tui             Browse provenance in an interactive viewer (TTY only)

item.stdout:
Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using hybrid search (semantic + keyword),
powered by the Entire search service.

Requires authentication via 'entire login' (GitHub device flow).

By default, results are scoped to the current repository. Use --all-repos to
search across all accessible repos.

Run without arguments to open an interactive search. Results are
displayed in an interactive table. Use --json for machine-readable output,
and add --compact for a trimmed per-result shape suited to agents (implies
--json): id, type, repo, branch, author, date, files touched, score, match
snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (repo hits add
description and checkpoint count). Fetch full detail
for a single result with 'entire checkpoint explain <id>', or add --full to
that command to pull the checkpoint's entire session transcript. For a
checkpoint hit from another GitHub repo, add --repo <owner/name> to
'entire checkpoint explain' (requires the full checkpoint ID; unrelated to
this command's --repo filter below).

CLI queries also support inline filters like author:<name>, date:<week|month>,
branch:<name>, repo:<owner/name>, and repo:* to search all accessible repos.

Usage:
  entire search [query] [flags]

Examples:
  entire search "retry backoff" --json
  entire search "retry backoff" --json --compact
  entire search "auth timeout author:alice date:week"
  entire search --code "parseToken"

Flags:
      --all-repos        Search all accessible repos instead of just the current one
      --author string    Filter by author name
      --branch string    Filter by branch name
      --case-sensitive   Case-sensitive code search (only with --code)
      --code             Search code content across repositories
      --compact          Trimmed JSON output for agents: id, repo, files touched, score, match snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (implies --json)
      --date string      Filter by time period (week or month)

item.stdout:
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo owner/name
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

Usage:
  entire checkpoint explain [checkpoint-id | commit-sha] [flags]

Flags:
  -c, --checkpoint string             Explain a specific checkpoint (ID or prefix)
      --commit string                 Explain a specific commit (SHA or ref, "commit-ish")
      --force                         Regenerate summary even if one already exists (requires --generate)
      --full                          Show full parsed transcript (all prompts/responses)
      --generate                      Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  -h, --help                          help for explain
      --insecure-http-auth            Allow plain-HTTP auth for --repo (local dev only)
      --json                          Output metadata as JSON (no transcript bytes)
      --limit int                     Cap the list view at N checkpoints (default: 100). Only meaningful with --json.
      --no-pager                      Disable pager output
      --raw-transcript                Show raw transcript file (JSONL format)
      --repo string                   Explain a checkpoint owned by another repo (owner/name or gh/owner/name), read from that repo's Entire API
      --search-all                    Search all commits (no branch/depth limit, may be slow)
      --session string                Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)
      --session-index int             Session index within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based, defaults to latest) (default -1)
  -s, --short                         Show summary only (omit prompts and files)
      --summary-timeout-seconds int   Hard deadline in seconds for --generate summary generation; overrides summary_timeout_seconds setting. 0 = use setting; if setting is also unset or 0, no automatic deadline applies.
      --transcript                    Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes to stdout

Global Flags:

item.stdout:
Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

Usage:
  entire api <path> [flags]

Examples:
  entire api /api/v1/clusters
  entire api --to cell /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --jurisdiction eu /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --to cell "/api/v1/me/recap?repo={repo_id}"
  entire api -X POST /api/v1/projects -f name=demo

Flags:
  -F, --field stringArray       add a typed parameter in key=value format; true/false/null/numbers are converted (repeatable)
  -H, --header stringArray      add a request header in key:value format (repeatable)
  -h, --help                    help for api
  -i, --include                 print the response status line and headers too
      --input string            file with the request body ("-" for stdin)
  -j, --jurisdiction string     target a specific jurisdiction's cell (e.g. us, eu) instead of your home cell; implies --to cell
  -X, --method string           HTTP method (default GET, or POST when a field/body is given)
  -f, --raw-field stringArray   add a string parameter in key=value format (repeatable)
      --to string               which backend to call: core or cell (default "core")

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo owner/name
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)

  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with

  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

7. Rank the strongest historical conflicts.
8. Output a concise, human-readable warning containing:
   - risk level,
   - detected conflict,
   - evidence,
   - commit/checkpoint when available,
   - affected file/symbol,
   - reason for the warning.
9. The command must be read-only.
10. Do not modify Entire core.
11. Do not modify checkpoint storage.
12. Do not create commits.
13. Do not push.

- Add unit tests for prompt/path/risk-term extraction.
- Add tests for ranking conflict-like results.
- Add a test for Entire-search failure with Git-history fallback.
- Add a test confirming the radar performs no repository writes.
- Keep tests deterministic and avoid requiring network/authentication.

Important:
- Follow existing repository conventions.
- Keep the implementation small and low-latency.
- Do not add Databricks yet; the radar core must work independently first.

content.text:
We are continuing the Codebase Flight Recorder buildathon project after the official Track 3 Noon Curveball.

Do NOT edit, create, delete, stage, commit, or push anything yet.

First reconstruct our pre-curveball state from the Entire checkpoint:
- Pre-curveball commit: 5bcfe14
- Pre-curveball Entire checkpoint: 2c466aa8c1e9
- Feature branch: feature/codex-integration

Use Entire checkpoint context/provenance to reconstruct:
1. Original intent
2. Architecture
3. Completed implementation
4. Open risks and assumptions

Then inspect the Track 3 curveball requirement:
- The integrated agent/workflow has changed transcript and lifecycle-event format.
- Support both original and new formats.
- Unknown events must not crash the integration.
- Incomplete transcripts must produce a partial result, not a corrupted/discarded session.
- Preserve existing checkpoint behavior.
- Tests must cover original format, new format, unknown events, and incomplete input.
- Do not duplicate the entire implementation for each format.

After reconstructing the checkpoint, perform Entire Graph impact analysis BEFORE any implementation.

Use Graph to identify affected:
- transcript parsers
- lifecycle handlers
- summary paths
- checkpoint writing paths
- Codex hook/radar integration paths

Clearly distinguish confirmed Graph relationships from heuristic/incomplete findings, and identify anything requiring source/test verification.

IMPORTANT:
- This is analysis only.
- Do not modify files yet.
- Do not commit or push.
- Do not resume the previous Codex session.
- Report the checkpoint reconstruction and Graph impact findings first.

The current native Codex transcript already shows `session_meta`, `event_msg`, `response_item`, `turn_context`, `world_state`, and `token_usage_record`; notably `response_item` can contain `encrypted_content`, and `event_msg.payload.item` nests lifecycle/tool records. That makes the curveball concrete: parser logic must tolerate wrapper variants and unknown top-level/event types without losing partial results.

Grok is the clearest existing example for the exact curveball properties: it already skips malformed JSONL lines, drops unknown message types by default, preserves one output line per input line during sanitization, and avoids truncating native session data on restore. I’m checking protocol and test hooks now to see where partial-result behavior is already expected versus missing.

    73	
    74	Two limitations are worth knowing before relying on it.
    75	
    76	**Resume is not full fidelity.** Grok records its reasoning state in an
    77	`encrypted_content` blob on every `reasoning` line. Entire strips that field before storing
    78	the transcript, so a resumed session replays the conversation, tool calls and results, but
    79	without Grok's prior reasoning context. Conversation recall is unaffected in testing; the
    80	effect on long or complex threads has not been characterised.
    81	
    82	The field is stripped for two reasons. It is large: a reasoning-heavy session produced
    83	values up to 12 KB each, around 15% of the transcript, and the transcript is re-stored on
    84	every checkpoint. And Entire's redactor treats it as a secret because it is high-entropy
    85	base64, corrupting it on restore and leaving a session Grok refuses to replay at all
    86	("This session's conversation history is incompatible with the current model"). Dropping
    87	the field avoids both problems, and Grok replays correctly without it. This mirrors what
    88	Entire already does for the built-in Codex agent.
    89	
    90	**Sessions captured before this behaviour shipped cannot be resumed.** Their stored
    91	transcripts already contain redaction-corrupted `encrypted_content`. Redaction is
    92	irreversible, so those sessions must be started fresh.
    93	
    94	Prefer `grok --resume <session-id>` over `grok --continue`. `--continue` picks whichever
    95	session Grok saw most recently in that directory, which may be a different one, and it
    96	resumes it without complaining.

# External Agent Builder

This repository includes a skill that guides you through building standalone external agent binaries for the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli). The current testing split is:

- Protocol compliance in `external-agents-tests`
- Lifecycle integration in this repo's `e2e/` harness
- Agent-specific unit tests in each `agents/entire-agent-*` module

## Available Commands

| Command | Skill file | Description |
|---------|-----------|-------------|
| Full pipeline | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` | Run all three phases sequentially |
| Research | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md` | Analyze the target agent's capabilities and map to the protocol |
| Write tests | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md` | Scaffold the binary and wire protocol compliance plus lifecycle coverage |
| Implement | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md` | Build the binary using protocol compliance first, lifecycle second, unit tests last |

## How to Use

When the user asks to "build an external agent", "create an agent binary", or "external agent plugin":

1. Read `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` for the full pipeline overview
2. Follow the three phases in order: research, write-tests, implement

Analysis only completed. I did not edit, stage, commit, push, or resume the previous Codex session.

**Checkpoint Reconstruction**
Pre-curveball state is commit `5bcfe14` on `feature/codex-integration`, with trailer `Entire-Checkpoint: 2c466aa8c1e9`.

Original intent:
Build a “Decision Conflict Radar” for the Codebase Flight Recorder Track 3 project. Its job is to warn before implementation when the current Codex prompt appears to conflict with prior history: reverted approaches, failed approaches, rejected decisions, or dependency/impact relationships.

Architecture:
The selected design was intentionally outside Entire core and outside checkpoint storage. It uses a standalone read-only Python command at [entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire_conflict_radar.py:1), wrapped by [entire-conflict-radar](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire-conflict-radar:1). Codex invokes it from `UserPromptSubmit` before the preserved Entire hook in [.codex/hooks.json](/home/hp/build/.codex/hooks.json:75).

Completed implementation:
`5bcfe14` added:
- [.codex/hooks.json](/home/hp/build/.codex/hooks.json:75): Codex hooks, including radar on `UserPromptSubmit` and existing `entire hooks codex user-prompt-submit`.
- [entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire_conflict_radar.py:154): prompt extraction, signal extraction, Entire search/code search, Git fallback, ranking, warning rendering, Codex `systemMessage`.
- [test_entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/test_entire_conflict_radar.py:23): deterministic tests for extraction, ranking, fallback, no writes, empty input, hook payload, and hook config.
- Commit stats: 4 files, 809 insertions.

Open risks and assumptions:
- Entire search/auth can fail; Git fallback is intentional but weaker.
- Current `extract_prompt_text` is generic and shallow. It supports direct fields like `user_prompt`, `userPrompt`, `prompt`, `message`, `content`, `input`, but it likely mishandles nested Codex content blocks with `{type, text}` because `text` is not preferred.
- Current `.entire/tmp/pre-prompt-...json` for this active session has `prompt:null`; the actual prompt is visible in native Codex JSONL as `response_item.payload.content[].text`. That is a concrete curveball risk.
- Existing checkpoint behavior depends on the preserved `entire hooks codex ...` commands; we should avoid changing them.

**Curveball Impact**
Confirmed Graph relationships:
- `entire why .codex/hooks.json:81 --json` maps the radar hook line to commit `5bcfe14`, checkpoint `2c466aa8c1e9`, session `01a07549-7d9a-7b43-945c-bf0ab08a54e1`.
- `entire why tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire_conflict_radar.py:154 --json` maps prompt extraction to the same checkpoint/session.
- `entire experts tools/entire-conflict-radar --branch feature/codex-integration --json` confirms Codex ownership of the radar files and checkpoint `2c466aa8c1e9`.
- `entire why agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/native_transcript.go:433 --json` maps Grok transcript sanitization to commit `c4c0eb99`, checkpoint `3b8de7933fe8`, though checkpoint metadata is missing locally.

Incomplete Graph findings:
- `entire graph` is not a valid command in this CLI.
- `entire experts .codex` returned no profiles even on `feature/codex-integration`, despite `entire why` resolving the hook line. Treat `.codex` graph coverage as incomplete.
- `entire experts agents/entire-agent-grok` returned no profiles, while `entire why` resolves specific Grok lines. Treat module-level Grok ownership as incomplete.

Affected source paths needing verification:
- Transcript/input parsers: [entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire_conflict_radar.py:154), [native_transcript.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/native_transcript.go:50), [native_transcript.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/native_transcript.go:278).
- Lifecycle handlers: [.codex/hooks.json](/home/hp/build/.codex/hooks.json:3), [hooks.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/hooks.go:21), [types.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/types.go:48).
- Summary paths: [entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire_conflict_radar.py:483), [transcript.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/transcript.go:246), [transcript.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/transcript.go:102).
- Checkpoint writing/validation paths: preserved Codex hook at [.codex/hooks.json](/home/hp/build/.codex/hooks.json:86), external-agent `WriteSession` at [transcript.go](/home/hp/build/agents/entire-agent-grok/internal/grok/transcript.go:81), checkpoint validation at [assertions.go](/home/hp/build/e2e/testutil/assertions.go:269).
- Codex hook/radar integration: [.codex/hooks.json](/home/hp/build/.codex/hooks.json:75), [entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/entire_conflict_radar.py:535), [test_entire_conflict_radar.py](/home/hp/build/tools/entire-conflict-radar/test_entire_conflict_radar.py:149).

Implementation implication, when allowed:
Add a normalization layer, not duplicate format-specific implementations. For radar, normalize hook/transcript JSON into canonical prompt text first, then reuse existing signal/search/ranking. Tests should cover direct original payloads, nested new `response_item`/`event_msg` payloads, unknown event records, malformed/incomplete JSON or JSONL, and no-warning empty input.

Analysis only. Do not edit, create, delete, stage, commit, or push anything.

The previous analysis reported that `entire graph` is not a valid command, but the buildathon guide requires Entire Graph impact analysis before implementation.

Now verify the installed Entire Graph surface using the CLI itself.

Run and inspect:
- entire graph version
- entire graph init-agents --repo .
- entire --help
- entire graph --help (if supported)
- any relevant Graph/search/relationship commands exposed by the installed CLI

Do not modify repository files. If `entire graph init-agents --repo .` would modify files, do not execute it; only inspect/help the command instead.

Report:
1. Which Graph commands actually exist in Entire CLI 0.10.5.
2. Which command can provide relationship/impact evidence for the affected paths.
3. What Graph evidence we can capture before implementation.
4. What remains unavailable/incomplete and therefore must be treated as heuristic.

I’ll keep this read-only and verify the Graph surface from the installed CLI rather than assuming from the prior `graph --help` failure. I’ll avoid running `init-agents` directly until its help confirms whether it writes files.

## Memory

You have access to a memory folder with guidance from prior runs. It can save
time and help you stay consistent. Use it whenever it is likely to help.

Decision boundary: should you use memory for a new user query?

- Skip memory ONLY when the request is clearly self-contained and does not need
  workspace history, conventions, or prior decisions.
- Hard skip examples: current time/date, simple translation, simple sentence
  rewrite, one-line shell command, trivial formatting.
- Use memory by default when ANY of these are true:
  - the query mentions workspace/repo/module/path/files in MEMORY_SUMMARY below,
  - the user asks for prior context / consistency / previous decisions,
  - the task is ambiguous and could depend on earlier project choices,
  - the ask is a non-trivial and related to MEMORY_SUMMARY below.
- If unsure, do a quick memory pass.

Memory layout (general -> specific):

- /home/hp/.codex/memories/memory_summary.md (already provided below; do NOT open again)
- /home/hp/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md (searchable registry; primary file to query)
- /home/hp/.codex/memories/skills/<skill-name>/ (skill folder)
  - SKILL.md (entrypoint instructions)
  - scripts/ (optional helper scripts)
  - examples/ (optional example outputs)
  - templates/ (optional templates)
- /home/hp/.codex/memories/rollout_summaries/ (per-rollout recaps + evidence snippets)
  - The paths of these entries can be found in /home/hp/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md or /home/hp/.codex/memories/rollout_summaries/ as `rollout_path`
  - These files are append-only `jsonl`: `session_meta.payload.id` identifies the session, `turn_context` marks turn boundaries, `event_msg` is the lightweight status stream, and `response_item` contains actual messages, tool calls, and tool outputs.
  - For efficient lookup, prefer matching the filename suffix or `session_meta.payload.id`; avoid broad full-content scans unless needed.

Quick memory pass (when applicable):

1. Skim the MEMORY_SUMMARY below and extract task-relevant keywords.
2. Search /home/hp/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md using those keywords.
3. Only if MEMORY.md directly points to rollout summaries/skills, open the 1-2
   most relevant files under /home/hp/.codex/memories/rollout_summaries/ or
   /home/hp/.codex/memories/skills/.
4. If above are not clear and you need exact commands, error text, or precise evidence, search over `rollout_path` for more evidence.
5. If there are no relevant hits, stop memory lookup and continue normally.

Quick-pass budget:

- Keep memory lookup lightweight: ideally <= 4-6 search steps before main work.
- Avoid broad scans of all rollout summaries.

During execution: if you hit repeated errors, confusing behavior, or suspect
relevant prior context, redo the quick memory pass.

How to decide whether to verify memory:

- Consider both risk of drift and verification effort.
- If a fact is likely to drift and is cheap to verify, verify it before
  answering.
- If a fact is likely to drift but verification is expensive, slow, or
  disruptive, it is acceptable to answer from memory in an interactive turn,
  but you should say that it is memory-derived, note that it may be stale, and
  consider offering to refresh it live.
- If a fact is lower-drift and expensive to verify, it is usually fine to
  answer from memory directly.

When answering from memory without current verification:

- If you rely on memory for a fact that you did not verify in the current turn,
  say so briefly in the final answer.
- If that fact is plausibly drift-prone or comes from an older note, older
  snapshot, or prior run summary, say that it may be stale or outdated.
- If live verification was skipped and a refresh would be useful in the
  interactive context, consider offering to verify or refresh it live.
- Do not present unverified memory-derived facts as confirmed-current.
- Prefer a short refresh offer for interactive questions, especially about prior
  results, commands, timing, or older snapshots.

Memory citation requirements:

- If ANY relevant memory files were used: append exactly one
`<oai-mem-citation>` block as the VERY LAST content of the final reply.
  Normal responses should include the answer first, then append the
`<oai-mem-citation>` block at the end.
- Use this exact structure for programmatic parsing:
```
<oai-mem-citation>
<citation_entries>
MEMORY.md:234-236|note=[responsesapi citation extraction code pointer]
rollout_summaries/2026-02-17T21-23-02-LN3m-example.md:10-12|note=[weekly report format]
</citation_entries>
<rollout_ids>
019c6e27-e55b-73d1-87d8-4e01f1f75043
019c7714-3b77-74d1-9866-e1f484aae2ab
</rollout_ids>
</oai-mem-citation>
```
- `citation_entries` is for rendering:
  - one citation entry per line
  - format: `<file>:<line_start>-<line_end>|note=[<how memory was used>]`
  - use file paths relative to the memory base path (for example, `MEMORY.md`,
    `rollout_summaries/...`, `skills/...`)
  - only cite files actually used under the memory base path (do not cite
    workspace files as memory citations)
  - if you used `MEMORY.md` and then a rollout summary/skill file, cite both
  - list entries in order of importance (most important first)
  - `note` should be short, single-line, and use simple characters only (avoid
    unusual symbols, no newlines)
- `rollout_ids` is for us to track what previous rollouts you find useful:
  - include one rollout id per line
  - rollout ids should look like UUIDs (for example,
    `019c6e27-e55b-73d1-87d8-4e01f1f75043`)
  - include unique ids only; do not repeat ids
  - an empty `<rollout_ids>` section is allowed if no rollout ids are available
  - you can find rollout ids in rollout summary files and MEMORY.md
  - do not include file paths or notes in this section
  - For every `citation_entries`, try to find and cite the corresponding rollout id if possible
- Never include memory citations inside pull-request messages.
- Never cite blank lines; double-check ranges.

You can update the memories **only** when explicitly asked by the user. This must always come from a direct request from the user.

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

# Freshworks Agentic Developer Toolkit

Managed install. Update with: `npx @freshworks/fw-dev-tools update`

## Update check (once per session)

On the first skill invocation of each session: run `bash ~/.fw-dev-tools/scripts/check-update.sh` and print its output if non-empty. Then proceed normally.

`check-update.sh` writes `update_check` fields (`lastChecked`, `lastNudged`, `latestVersion`, `updateAvailable`) to **`~/.fw-dev-tools/.meta.json`** (install state). Do **not** write `update_check` to per-app `<app-dir>/.meta.json` — that file is for skill metrics only (`meta-init.sh` / `meta-update.sh`).

## IDE skill paths (MANDATORY)

Read fw-dev-tools skills **only** from the install path for your IDE. Never mix paths across IDEs.

| IDE | Skill path |
|---|---|
| **Cursor** | `~/.cursor/skills/fw-<name>/SKILL.md` |
| **Codex** | `~/.codex/skills/fw-<name>/SKILL.md` |
| **Claude Code** | `~/.fw-dev-tools/skills/fw-<name>/SKILL.md` — loaded via installed plugin (`/fw-<name>`); |

## Which skill to use

| Goal | Skill |
|---|---|
| Build, fix, review, or migrate a Platform 3.0 app | `skills/fw-app-dev/SKILL.md` |
| AI Actions integrations (actions.json, SMI, request templates) | `skills/fw-ai-actions-app/SKILL.md` |
| Structured app review (iparams, frontend, script checks, report) | `skills/fw-review/SKILL.md` |
| Install, upgrade, or troubleshoot FDK and Node (nvm, PATH) | `skills/fw-setup/SKILL.md` |
| Publish a built app to the marketplace | `skills/fw-publish/SKILL.md` |

**End-to-end order:** fw-setup → fw-app-dev / fw-ai-actions-app → fw-review (MANDATORY) → fw-publish

## Non-negotiables

- Platform version `"3.0"`; use `modules` not legacy `product`
- New UI apps: React Meta default (`metaConfig.framework: "react"`, DEW); vanilla Crayons only when explicitly requested
- External HTTP only via `$request.invokeTemplate` and `config/requests.json` templates
- `fdk validate`: zero platform errors and zero lint errors before complete
- fw-review is MANDATORY before fw-publish — never skip it
- Per-app `<app-dir>/.meta.json`: write **only** via `meta-init.sh` / `meta-update.sh` (and `meta-feedback.sh` / `meta-delete.sh` for publish) — **never** hand-write or Edit/Write the file; `skill_version` from the active skill's `SKILL.md` `version:` field, not `plugin.json`
- DEPRECATED MCP tools (do NOT use): `implement_app`, `get_implementation_plan`, `idea_to_app`, `fix_app_errors`

<!-- fw-dev-tools end -->

# External Agent Builder

This repository includes a skill that guides you through building standalone external agent binaries for the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli). The current testing split is:

- Protocol compliance in `external-agents-tests`
- Lifecycle integration in this repo's `e2e/` harness
- Agent-specific unit tests in each `agents/entire-agent-*` module

## Available Commands

| Command | Skill file | Description |
|---------|-----------|-------------|
| Full pipeline | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` | Run all three phases sequentially |
| Research | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md` | Analyze the target agent's capabilities and map to the protocol |
| Write tests | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md` | Scaffold the binary and wire protocol compliance plus lifecycle coverage |
| Implement | `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md` | Build the binary using protocol compliance first, lifecycle second, unit tests last |

## How to Use

When the user asks to "build an external agent", "create an agent binary", or "external agent plugin":

1. Read `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` for the full pipeline overview
2. Follow the three phases in order: research, write-tests, implement
3. Each phase has a dedicated skill file with detailed instructions
4. Keep reusable protocol checks out of this repo's `e2e/` directory. Add them to `external-agents-tests` instead.

## Tool Mapping (Codex)

The skill files reference Claude Code tool names. Map them to Codex equivalents:

| Skill references | Codex equivalent |

| `Task` / subagent launches | Codex's native subagent system |

### How to use skills

- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):
  1) After deciding to use a skill, the main agent must expand the listed short `path` with the matching alias from `### Skill roots`, then open and read its `SKILL.md` completely before taking task actions. If a read is truncated or paginated, continue until EOF.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the directory containing that expanded `SKILL.md` first, and only consider other paths if needed.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, use its routing instructions to identify the files required for the task. The main agent must read each required instruction or reference file itself before acting on it. Do not delegate reading, summarizing, or interpreting skill instructions to a subagent. Subagents may still perform task work when the selected skill allows it.
  4) If `scripts/` exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.
  5) If `assets/` or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Progressive disclosure applies to selecting relevant files, not partially reading a selected instruction file. Do not load unrelated references, scripts, or assets.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer opening only files directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless you're blocked.
  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

Implement the Track 3 Noon Curveball requirement while preserving the existing Decision Conflict Radar behavior.

Curveball:
- The integrated agent/workflow has changed transcript and lifecycle-event format.
- Support both the original and new format.
- Unknown events must not crash the integration.
- Incomplete transcripts must produce a partial result, not a corrupted/discarded session.
- Preserve existing Entire checkpoint behavior.
- Do not duplicate the implementation for each format.

Design constraint:
Create ONE normalization layer that converts supported Codex hook/transcript inputs into a canonical internal representation. Reuse the existing extraction, signal detection, search, ranking, and warning logic after normalization.

Specifically address the risk identified during checkpoint reconstruction:
- Existing extraction handles direct fields such as user_prompt, userPrompt, prompt, message, content, and input.
- New Codex records may contain nested content blocks such as response_item.payload.content[].text.

- Unknown event records must be safely ignored.
- Malformed or truncated JSON/JSONL must be treated as incomplete input and must never cause the radar to crash.
